6.0.0.en: 1 Hear ye now what the LORD saith; Arise, contend thou before the mountains, and let the hills hear thy voice. 2 Hear ye, O mountains, the LORD's controversy, and ye strong foundations of the earth: for the LORD hath a controversy with his people, and he will plead with Israel. 3 O my people, what have I done unto thee? and wherein have I wearied thee? testify against me. 4 For I brought thee up out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed thee out of the house of servants; and I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. 5 O my people, remember now what Balak king of Moab consulted, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him from Shittim unto Gilgal; that ye may know the righteousness of the LORD. 6 Wherewith shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before the high God? shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves of a year old? 7 Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? 8 He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?

6.0.1.en: Hear ye now what the LORD saith;

6.0.2.en: Arise, contend thou before the mountains, and let the hills hear thy voice. [1]

6.0.3.en: God asks the prophet Micah to arise and declare the controversy against the stubborn people, asking the mountains and hills to listen and follow the trial.

6.0.4.en: Chapters 6 and 7 depict a courtroom, where God judges in order to move His people to repentance before the great day of judgment comes.

6.0.5.en: The prophet Micah affirms that what he utters is not from himself, but that he drew it from God; he does not present a human word, but the word of the Holy God. For this reason it is fitting that they listen and give heed.

6.0.6.en: God calls the mountains and hills to stand as witnesses against His people, who built idolatrous altars on the high places, and offered sacrifices to strange, vain gods (1 Kgs 14:23; Jer 17:2-3; Ezek 20:27-28). Perhaps He means to bring the controversy against the inhabitants of those mountains and hills, which were immersed in idol worship.

6.0.7.en: Hear ye, O mountains, the LORD's controversy, and ye strong foundations of the earth:

6.1.0.en: for the LORD hath a controversy with his people, and he will plead with Israel. [2]

6.1.1.en: He cries aloud and does not keep silent (Isa 58:1), so that the foundations of the earth may hear him, for the matter is extremely serious. If the hearts of the people have become like hard rocks, God calls the rocks of the earth to listen and rebuke His people, because Israel has ears and does not hear.

6.1.2.en: "The LORD hath a controversy with his people": sin is turning the back to God, and so it becomes a cause of controversy with God. For this reason the Apostle Paul says: "when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God" (Rom 5:10).

6.1.3.en: If sin in general causes controversy with the Holy One, who cannot bear sin, it does so all the more when it proceeds from His people and His children, whom He wants to be holy to Him, as He is holy (Lev 20:26).

6.1.4.en: "He will plead with Israel," which some translate "He will reason with Israel": He wants to enter into dialogue with His people in order to affirm to them His gift of "free will," and so that they may look to His holy commandment not as an issued order they find hard, but as a work of love proceeding from a heavenly Father toward His beloved children.

6.1.5.en: * In many cases in the Holy Scriptures you see this picture, which is very astonishing and befits the tender love of God. He proclaims His ineffable goodness by showing that He wishes to enter into judgment with humanity in a wonderful manner.

6.1.6.en: St. John Chrysostom. * Thus He judges them, but hear what followed concerning the believers: "He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us" (Mic 7:19)... The Scripture says: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted" (Mt 5:5). And in another place the words: "He that believeth on me is not condemned, but is passed from death unto life, and he that believeth not is condemned."

6.1.7.en: Cassiodorus. O my people, what have I done unto thee?

6.1.8.en: and wherein have I wearied thee?

6.2.1.en: God did not issue His judgment against His people, though He is the almighty Judge, but He asks to reason with them. He asks them whether He has wronged them in anything. By what do they justify their unfaithfulness to Him in spite of His surpassing faithfulness toward them.

6.2.2.en: It was not possible for the people to answer this question, because God, who is all love and mercy, has not wronged and never will wrong the people, nor any man, for He is the merciful Maker of good things, and if He permits affliction or chastening, it is for our proving or for our repentance and return to Him. He is not a harsh master, but a loving Father.

6.2.3.en: * Do you wish me to speak to you with the very words of God to stiff-necked and hard Israel? "O my people, what have I done unto thee? and wherein have I harmed thee? and wherein have I wearied thee?" This language is in truth more fitting for me to direct to you who have wronged me. It is grievous that we seek occasions against one another and break the fellowship of the Spirit that we have by differences of opinion, so that each has become more savage and violent against the other than the barbarians who are now fighting us, who have joined together against us by the Trinity that we divided... We have come to be at war, one against another, even against those of the one household. Or, if you will, we, members of one body, perish and destroy one another.

6.2.4.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus. * "O my people, what have I done unto thee? and wherein have I wearied thee?" (Mic 6:3), showing their ingratitude, for while they enjoy all things, they meet Him with the opposite.

6.3.0.en: St. John Chrysostom. For I brought thee up out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed thee out of the house of servants; and I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. [4]

6.3.1.en: Since the people were silent for their inability to answer, God reviewed His dealings of love toward them from the time they were enslaved in Egypt, and how He sent them leaders supported by His grace: Moses, great among the prophets, and Aaron, the first high priest, and Miriam, the leader of the women, to create an atmosphere of joy through praise.

6.4.0.en: O my people, remember now what Balak king of Moab consulted, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him from Shittim unto Gilgal; that ye may know the righteousness of the LORD. [5]

6.4.1.en: God's care for His people continued in the wilderness, and how He kept them from the plots of Balak king of Moab so that they might cross over and enter the land of promise. He is faithful always.

6.4.2.en: The prophet Moses recorded the story of Balak and Balaam in the Book of Numbers (Num 22-24).

6.4.3.en: Shittim: the place where the children of Israel pitched their tents on the eastern bank of the Jordan before crossing the river to enter the land of promise (Josh 2:1). There the people received many divine commandments and promises. As for Gilgal, it was the first place where the people encamped after crossing the Jordan (Josh 5:3-3). There the people renewed their covenant with God (Josh 5:3-9).

6.4.4.en: St. Ambrose sees that God presents Himself to us as an example from which we learn, for even while rebuking His people He reminds them of His care for them when they were in affliction under slavery in a foreign land, burdened with heavy loads.

6.4.5.en: Wherewith shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before the high God?

6.5.0.en: shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves of a year old? [6]

6.5.1.en: The Jews thought they were able to appease God by the multitude of sacrifices without practicing the spiritual life in their daily conduct. As though what concerns God were the offerings and sacrifices presented to Him in His temple, they did not realize that God seeks man himself: "My son, give me thine heart, and let thine eyes observe my ways." God wants to prepare us to enjoy fellowship in the eternal glories. God wants us to offer living, reasonable sacrifices, acceptable to Him (Rom 12:1-2). Sacrifices of love from the heart, so that we return love to Him with love!

6.5.2.en: Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil?

6.6.0.en: shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? [7]

6.6.1.en: Israel's first answer came in the form of three questions: First, is God pleased with the offering of ordinary calves as sacrifices? Second, will He multiply the sacrifices and offerings, so that he slaughters thousands of rams and offers ten thousands of rivers of oil? Third, will he offer extraordinary sacrifices, even if it leads to offering their firstborn (of their sons) as sacrifices, which the Law forbids (Deut 12:29-31; 2 Kgs 3:27; Judg 11:30-40)? For the sacrifice of the firstborn son had crept into Israel along with other sinful idolatrous practices.

6.6.2.en: It is clear that the sinner, however much sin attracts him, feels a deep emptiness in the depths of his soul, and wants to fill this emptiness by appeasing God, even if he offers all that he possesses, and what is most precious to him: his children! But the need is for the sanctification of the heart and mind and practical conduct in the Lord!

6.6.3.en: * God is not reconciled, nor are sins forgiven, by ten thousands of goats and thousands of rams or by the fruits of unholiness; rather the grace of the Lord shows the good life.

6.6.4.en: St. Ambrose. * Does everyone who turns from sin to faith turn from sinful practices (as if they were his mother) to life? I cite one of the twelve prophets, who says: "Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?" (Mic 6:7). Can a mother buy her way to God by offering her firstborn? This must not be understood as an attack on the words: "Be fruitful, and multiply" (Gen 1:28).

6.6.5.en: St. Clement of Alexandria. * When they were rebuked because they always lacked any other virtue, they excused themselves at first that they offer sacrifices, saying that they offer them continually. From here we understand why all the prophets exactly... reject this defense. For it is clear that the sacrifices were not established for their own sake, but as an instrument to suggest their conduct. So if they ignored their necessary obligations, occupied only with sacrifices, God said that He no longer accepts them (Amos 5:22; Isa 1:11-15).

6.7.0.en: Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus. He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God? [8]

6.7.1.en: Israel thought it pleased God with animal sacrifices and the multitude of offerings, even to the point of offering human sacrifices, so the prophet arose to correct their concepts by moving them from preoccupation with animal sacrifices while practicing injustice to the practice of active love and walking humbly with the Lord.

6.7.2.en: As God was preparing the mind of His people to accept the Gentiles into the faith, the answer came general to any man in the world: "He hath shewed thee, O man," and He did not say "O Israel." The message is directed to all.

6.7.3.en: * Now, it is our duty to live the virtuous life, and God asks this of us; we do not rely on Him or on another, nor, as some think, on fate, but it is from our work, as the saying of the prophet Micah demonstrates: "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy" (Mic 6:8).

6.7.4.en: Origen the scholar. * Who is so foolish as to think that God needs what is offered to Him for His own use? In many places He makes this idea foolish. So as not to trouble you, it is enough for me to quote this brief saying from the Psalm: "I said unto the LORD, Thou art my God: my goodness extendeth not to thee" (Ps 26:2). It is fitting for us to believe that God has no need not only of a flock or any earthly material thing, but not even of man's righteousness, and that any right worship offered to God is not for His benefit but for the benefit of man. For no one says that a spring benefits from his drinking of it, nor the light from his seeing it. In fact the ancient Church offered animal sacrifices, which the present people of God read about without imitating them, for these sacrifices mean nothing except that they point to what we do in order to cleave to God and urge our neighbor to do so. The sacrifice is a visible sacrament or holy sign of an invisible sacrifice.

6.7.5.en: * You ask: What ought I to offer? Offer yourself. For what does the Lord ask of you but yourself? For He created nothing among earthly creatures that is better than you. He asks of you yourself from yourself.

6.7.6.en: St. Augustine. * "God is good and exceedingly kind." He is merciful and gracious and rich in mercy (Ps 145:8). He does not desire the death of the wicked, but that he turn (Ezek 18:23). He is the Savior of all people, especially of those that believe (1 Tim 4:10). For this reason it is fitting for the children of God also to be merciful (Mt 5:7) and peacemakers (Mt 5:9), forgiving one another as Christ forgave us (Col 3:13), not judging lest we be judged (Mt 7:1), for a man stands or falls to God; who art thou that judgest another man's servant? (Rom 14:14).

6.7.7.en: Tertullian the scholar. * You have been told, O man, what is good, what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with your Lord? For this reason the Gospel says to you: "Arise, let us go hence" (Jn 14:31), while the Law says to you: "that you walk after the Lord your God." You have learned the way of escape from here; why do you delay?

6.7.8.en: St. Ambrose. * If God is fire, a consuming fire (Deut 4:24), then everyone who is straw, everyone who is wood, flees from the fire lest he be burned.2

6.7.9.en: St. Jerome. * He says: Forget your burnt offerings and your countless sacrifices, and the offerings of your firstborn. If you are concerned to appease the Godhead, practice what God commanded you at the beginning through Moses. What is this? That you have just judgment and sound decisions in all cases, where you choose what is better, not what is worse, so that you continue to bear witness to every possibility of love and feeling for the brotherhood of your neighbor, and that you be ready to practice what pleases God in every way. He means: "Love God with all your heart and all your mind and all your soul, and love your neighbor as yourself" (Deut 6:5; Lev 19:18), as was said of old by Moses. He says: Do this as a thing better than sacrifices in the eyes of God.

6.7.10.en: Theodore of Mopsuestia. * What is the benefit if you abstain from birds and fish while you bite your brethren and devour them? For the evil speaker eats the flesh of his brother and bites the body of his neighbor. For this reason Paul utters a dreadful saying: "But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another" (Gal 5:15). You do not fix your teeth in flesh, but you fix slander upon the soul, and cause a wound that is an evil suspicion; you hurt yourself in a thousand ways, and hurt others with you. For by your slander of your neighbor you make the one who listens to your slander fall into a bad state. If he is wicked, you make him indifferent to his evil, since he finds one who shares his evil. And if he is righteous, you lift him up to pride and arrogance, as the sins of others appear to him and he reckons himself to be something!

6.8.0.en: 9 The LORD's voice crieth unto the city, and the man of wisdom shall see thy name: hear ye the rod, and who hath appointed it. 10 Are there yet the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure that is abominable? 11 Shall I count them pure with the wicked balances, and with the bag of deceitful weights? 12 For the rich men thereof are full of violence, and the inhabitants thereof have spoken lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth. 13 Therefore also will I make thee sick in smiting thee, in making thee desolate because of thy sins. 14 Thou shalt eat, but not be satisfied; and thy casting down shall be in the midst of thee; and thou shalt take hold, but shalt not deliver; and that which thou deliverest will I give up to the sword. 15 Thou shalt sow, but thou shalt not reap; thou shalt tread the olives, but thou shalt not anoint thee with oil; and sweet wine, but shalt not drink wine. 16 For the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of the house of Ahab, and ye walk in their counsels; that I should make thee a desolation, and the inhabitants thereof an hissing: therefore ye shall bear the reproach of my people.

6.8.1.en: In the first session the controversy was before the mountains and hills; in the second He summoned the city of Jerusalem and with it wisdom, to witness and to fear His holy name.

6.8.2.en: The LORD's voice crieth unto the city, and the man of wisdom shall see thy name:

6.8.3.en: hear ye the rod, and who hath appointed it. [9]

6.8.4.en: Some translate "wisdom" as "those who have wisdom": when the Lord calls to the city, those who have wisdom can see His name, that is, discern it and recognize me, and His word works in them.

6.8.5.en: Perhaps he means here "the rod of divine chastening": before it falls upon the believer, it speaks, and if the believer hears it in a spirit of contrition and humility, it does not fall upon him. Let us hear the words of the One who appointed it, that is, the plans for chastening, and thus we enjoy the divine mercies.

6.9.0.en: Are there yet the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure that is abominable? [10]

6.9.1.en: What are the words of the divine rod of chastening? They are a disclosure of the injustice they practice against their brethren. Here he reviews an ancient issue that has afflicted humanity through the generations, namely the practice of injustice by the rich against the poor, as they think they are growing richer, but they are storing up treasures of wickedness and dishonesty. It is the issue of financial, social and moral corruption, in spite of the Lord's warnings to us.

6.9.2.en: If the unjust man thinks he has gathered abundant treasures, he has only gathered treasures of wickedness that come upon his own soul, and if he thinks that by his cheating in the balances he has obtained many good things, he has obtained a curse! The wise man says: "Treasures of wickedness profit nothing: but righteousness delivereth from death" (Prov 10:2).

6.10.0.en: Shall I count them pure with the wicked balances, and with the bag of deceitful weights? [11]

6.10.1.en: He means cheating in the narrow literal sense, where they cheat the simple in the balances; and he means cheating in its wide sense, where they deceive the simple with deceitful words and deceptive ways in order to seize their fields.

6.11.0.en: For the rich men thereof are full of violence, and the inhabitants thereof have spoken lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth. [12]

6.11.1.en: It is not strange to see unjust rich men, for the more a man receives, the more his greed for hoarding increases, unless his soul is satisfied within. For the abundance of possessions does not quench the inner thirst.

6.11.2.en: He speaks of greedy rich men whose hearts are filled with injustice, as their storehouses are filled with what they obtained unjustly. Injustice drives them to lie and resort to deceit to achieve what they desire. Their tongue utters deceit; they deceive themselves, "for they say, The LORD seeth us not; the LORD hath forsaken the earth" (Ezek 8:12).

6.11.3.en: * Let the mouth hasten in flight from shameful talk.

6.11.4.en: St. John Chrysostom. The Psalmist says: "Thou hatest all workers of iniquity. Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing: the LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man" (Ps 5:5-7).

6.11.5.en: * Every proud man is deceitful, and every deceitful man is a liar. Men toil when they speak vanity, but he who speaks the truth speaks with complete ease... He who wishes to speak the truth does not grow weary, because the truth itself speaks without weariness.3

6.12.0.en: St. Augustine. Therefore also will I make thee sick in smiting thee, in making thee desolate because of thy sins. [13]

6.12.1.en: The sentence is passed on those who persist in injustice, cheating and lying, that incurable sickness clings to them. For if they think that what they obtain satisfies their longings, they suffer from an inner disease that is hard to cure, namely the constant feeling of emptiness and lack of peace.

6.12.2.en: * "Thou hatest all workers of iniquity. Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing" (Ps 5:5-6). The worker of iniquity is hated by God; and the liar is destroyed. Come, let us see which of the two conditions is worse, that God hates him or that he is destroyed. He whom God hates is indeed unhappy, for he lives in enmity with God, yet he is still alive (his repentance may be hoped for); but the liar is destroyed and exists no more. Sadly, he who lies is worse than the worker of iniquity... "The mouth that lieth slayeth the soul" (Wis 1:11).3

6.12.3.en: St. Jerome. Thou shalt eat, but not be satisfied;

6.13.0.en: and thy casting down shall be in the midst of thee; and thou shalt take hold, but shalt not deliver; and that which thou deliverest will I give up to the sword. [14]

6.13.1.en: They eat but are not satisfied, because they mixed their food with evil, and so deprived themselves of the divine blessings. The feeling of hunger does not leave them, however much they eat and obtain. "[who] enlargeth his desire as hell... and cannot be satisfied" (Hab 2:5). "Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not?" (Isa 55:2). "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity" (Eccl 5:10).

6.13.2.en: "And thou shalt take hold (grasp), but shalt not deliver" [14]. However much the unjust man grasps what belongs to others and reckons that he has acquired it, he soon finds that it has slipped from his hands and fled, and he could not save it. What the unjust man holds tightly so that it does not escape from his hands, he loses quickly. And what he thinks very dear to him is lost to him, and even if the unjust man uses every means to keep his unjust money, the divine sword tears it apart, and it is as nothing.

6.13.3.en: * The greedy man is not rich. He is in want of many things, and while he is in need of much he cannot be rich. He is a keeper of wealth and not its master. He is a slave and not a prince. For he is ready to give a part of his body and not give from his buried gold... Surely this is not his own, because he is unable to decide to give to others, nor to distribute the necessities, but he treasures up for himself endless punishments, so how can it be his? He possesses these things which he is not free to use or to enjoy.

6.13.4.en: St. John Chrysostom. Thou shalt sow, but thou shalt not reap;

6.14.0.en: thou shalt tread the olives, but thou shalt not anoint thee with oil; and sweet wine, but shalt not drink wine. [15]

6.14.1.en: The unjust man thinks he sows in order to reap, but soon his seed withers and his work is scattered, so that he reaps nothing. He may gather olives and tread them in the press so that his storehouses are filled with oil, but he does not anoint himself with oil, either because his olives do not yield oil, or he loses the oil they yield. So also with the sweet wine (grape juice): even if he presses grapes he does not drink wine. In other words, God may permit the unjust man to lose all that he gathered, and if He leaves him the wealth that fills his storehouses, He strikes him so that he gets no benefit from this wealth, and his storehouses are full of oil and wine but he is unable to anoint his body with oil or drink a cup of wine!

6.15.0.en: For the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of the house of Ahab, and ye walk in their counsels; that I should make thee a desolation, and the inhabitants thereof an hissing: therefore ye shall bear the reproach of my people. [16]

6.15.1.en: Omri and Ahab are grave examples (1 Kgs 16:22) of greed and injustice; they used their authority to rob the poor, and obtained nothing!

6.15.2.en: When Omri reigned over Israel he led the people to the worship of idols (1 Kgs 21:16-26). And his son Ahab came, the most wicked of the kings of Israel (1 Kgs 16:2-33).

6.15.3.en: "That I should make thee a desolation, and the inhabitants thereof an hissing" [16]. Evil ruins the nation and destroys it, so that she becomes a reproach, which the gloating nations mock, hissing in derision. What makes matters worse is that this happens to the people of God; instead of enjoying the divine glories before the heavenly ones, they become a reproach before the pagan nations, and even descend to eternal shame on the great day of the Lord (Dan 12:2).

6.15.5.en: * If You, O Lord, were to judge, who would be justified before You?

6.15.6.en: Behold, heaven and earth bear witness to Your work with me!

6.15.7.en: Your works are surpassing, and Your love is marvelous!

6.15.8.en: Tell me how I may be proved righteous before You?

6.15.9.en: * You brought me out of the slavery of the devil, and carried me to the freedom of the glory of the children of God!

6.15.10.en: As You brought Your people out of the slavery of the devil, and brought them into the land of promise!

6.15.11.en: You shattered the devil's resistance to my salvation, as You frustrated the plot of Balaam, who loved the wages of unrighteousness.

6.15.12.en: * Tell me, with what shall I please You, O my God?

6.15.13.en: You have no need of my offerings nor of my gifts, for heaven and earth are the work of Your hands!

6.15.14.en: You have no need of my prayers and my worship, for You are all glorious in Yourself!

6.15.15.en: * Truly You seek me, not what I have; You seek my heart and make it a heaven, and You seek my mind to fill it with Your mysteries, and You seek my love for my brethren to pour love upon me!

6.15.16.en: You seek that I walk with You humbly, and so You lift me up to Your heavens!

6.15.17.en: * I confess to You every corruption that has crept into me!

6.15.18.en: Remove from me the balances of cheating and deceitful words, remove from me all injustice and selfishness.

6.15.19.en: For the world is unable to satisfy my soul.

6.15.20.en: And sin clothes me with shame and disgrace!

6.15.21.en: * You alone are everything to me.

6.15.22.en: I possess You, so I possess the truth; I am satisfied with You, so I shall not hunger; I carry You within me and am filled with the splendor of Your glory.

6.15.23.en: You are all to me, and with You I seek nothing!
